1291.quote_or_event: “My mind longs for the Blessed Vision of the Guru's Darshan.”
1291.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a mind that runs of its own accord toward the one it loves, longing only to see him.
1291.tie_back: The Kural's heart has already gone over to the beloved and will not stay with the speaker; Guru Arjan's mind likewise belongs wholly to the one it longs for.
1291.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1291._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; strong fit for a heart that runs to the beloved, but the Kural adds a reproach to the heart that Gurbani lacks, and the longing is for the Guru. This is spiritual love for God, not romantic love.

1292.quote_or_event: “If You seat me near You, then I worship and adore You. Even if You beat me and drive me out, I will still meditate on You.”
1292.explanation: Guru Ram Das says the devotee's love does not depend on how the Lord treats him; welcomed or driven away, he keeps turning to God.
1292.tie_back: Like the Kural's heart that goes to the beloved even when he shows no care, the devotee's heart keeps going to God whatever the treatment.
1292.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1292._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; close on the theme of love that persists without return; the Kural's speaker resents this in her heart, while Gurbani praises it. This is spiritual love for God, not romantic love.

1293.quote_or_event: “Emotional attachment to children and spouse is poison; in the end, no one will go along with you as your helper.”
1293.explanation: Guru Ram Das warns that worldly ties do not stay with us when we most need them.
1293.tie_back: The Kural quotes the proverb that the ruined have no friends and feels even her heart has left her; Gurbani makes the same point that no worldly companion stays to the end.
1293.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 41, Siree Raag, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1293._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; next-best: shares the idea that companions fail one in need, but Gurbani's point is detachment and reliance on God, not a lover's complaint against her own heart.

1294.quote_or_event: “The fickle mind continuously runs after fleeting things.”
1294.explanation: Guru Nanak describes a mind that will not stay put or follow sound counsel but chases whatever draws it.
1294.tie_back: The Kural's speaker complains that her heart will not keep to her plan of sulking first; Gurbani likewise names the restless mind that cannot be held to any plan.
1294.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 222, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1294._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; next-best: both describe an unruly heart that will not cooperate, but the Kural's context is a playful lovers' quarrel and Gurbani's is the mind's chase of worldly things.

1295.quote_or_event: “Without Him, I cannot survive even for an instant, and my life-night passes in anguish.”
1295.explanation: Guru Amar Das voices the soul-bride's constant pain while she is apart from her Lord.
1295.tie_back: The Kural's heart is never free of fear, dreading his absence and then dreading his leaving; Guru Amar Das likewise describes a soul in unbroken anguish over separation.
1295.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 35, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1295._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; good match for separation-anguish, but Gurbani has no counterpart for the second fear (dread of losing the beloved once present). This is spiritual love for God, not romantic love.

1296.quote_or_event: “The beautiful song-bird sings, perched on the mango tree; but how can I endure the pain in the depths of my being?”
1296.explanation: In his Barah Maha (song of the twelve months), Guru Nanak's soul-bride sits alone in spring and finds the beauty around her only deepens her inner pain.
1296.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker whose own heart seems to devour her when she sits alone thinking of her husband, Guru Nanak's bride is consumed from within by longing.
1296.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhaari (Barah Maha), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1296._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; reasonable fit for inner pain in solitude; the Kural's heart turns against her (and some commentators say she dwells on his faults), which Gurbani does not echo. This is spiritual love for God, not romantic love.

1297.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. ... give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
1297.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that true love for God means giving up concern for what people say, even giving one's head.
1297.tie_back: The Kural's speaker has lost her modesty to a heart that cannot forget her beloved; Guru Nanak says the path of love requires leaving behind the shame of public opinion.
1297.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1297._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; lines joined with an ellipsis (one intervening line omitted); good thematic link of love overriding social shame, but the Kural laments losing modesty while Gurbani calls for courage. This is spiritual love for God, not romantic love.

1298.quote_or_event: “Some sing of His Glorious Virtues, Greatness and Beauty.”
1298.explanation: In Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak describes devotees who dwell on God's qualities and beauty in praise.
1298.tie_back: The Kural's loving heart refuses to scorn the beloved and dwells on his good qualities instead; Japji describes the devotee's heart dwelling on the Lord's virtues.
1298.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1298._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; next-best: shares the act of dwelling on the beloved's good qualities, but Japji's line is general praise, without the Kural's struggle against reproach.

1299.quote_or_event: “He alone is called your companion, who will not be separated from you, here or hereafter.”
1299.explanation: Guru Arjan defines a true companion as the one who never leaves, which in Gurbani is God (and His Name).
1299.tie_back: The Kural asks who will stand by us in sorrow if our own heart does not; Gurbani answers that the only sure companion is the One who never departs.
1299.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 677, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1299._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; strong fit on the question of who truly stands by one; Gurbani's answer (God) differs from the Kural's focus on one's own heart.

1300.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
1300.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that mastering one's own mind is the key that sets right one's relation to the whole world.
1300.tie_back: The Kural says that when one's own heart is not kin, strangers will not be either; Japji likewise makes the mind the starting point for everything outside it.
1300.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1300._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) this session; reasonable match: both put one's own mind first, though Japji speaks of self-mastery and the Kural of a heart that fails its owner.
